def move_one_ball(arr):
    """We have an array 'arr' of N integers arr[1], arr[2], ..., arr[N].The
    numbers in the array will be randomly ordered. Your task is to determine if
    it is possible to get an array sorted in non-decreasing order by performing 
    the following operation on the given array:
        You are allowed to perform right shift operation any number of times.
    
    One right shift operation means shifting all elements of the array by one
    position in the right direction. The last element of the array will be moved to
    the starting position in the array i.e. 0th index. 

    If it is possible to obtain the sorted array by performing the above operation
    then return True else return False.
    If the given array is empty then return True.

    Note: The given list is guaranteed to have unique elements.

    For Example:
    
    move_one_ball([3, 4, 5, 1, 2])==>True
    Explanation: By performin 2 right shift operations, non-decreasing order can
                 be achieved for the given array.
    move_one_ball([3, 5, 4, 1, 2])==>False
    Explanation:It is not possible to get non-decreasing order for the given
                array by performing any number of right shift operations.
                
    """
    # Handle edge cases
    if len(arr) == 0 or len(arr) == 1:
        return True
    
    # Count the number of break points where arr[i] > arr[i+1]
    break_points = 0
    break_index = -1
    
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        next_i = (i + 1) % len(arr)
        if arr[i] > arr[next_i]:
            break_points += 1
            break_index = i
    
    # If there are no break points, array is already sorted
    if break_points == 0:
        return True
    
    # If there's more than one break point, cannot be sorted by rotation
    if break_points > 1:
        return False
    
    # If there's exactly one break point, verify it's a valid rotation
    # The array should be sorted if we rotate at break_index + 1
    # This means: arr[break_index+1:] + arr[:break_index+1] should be sorted
    # Which is equivalent to checking:
    # 1. Elements from break_index+1 to end are sorted (already checked above)
    # 2. Elements from 0 to break_index are sorted (already checked above)
    # 3. The last element should be <= first element (wraparound check)
    
    # Since we have exactly one break point at break_index,
    # we need to verify that arr[break_index+1] (the start of rotated array)
    # is the minimum and arr[break_index] (the end of rotated array) is compatible
    
    # The break point is at break_index, so the rotation would start at break_index+1
    # For this to work: arr[-1] <= arr[0] (last element <= first element after rotation)
    return arr[-1] <= arr[break_index]
